definitions.text: Wow; no way; that's incredible. The all-purpose exclamation for anything surprising, good or bad.
As a noun, a runaway success — a film, a shop or a business that has hit the jackpot. 대박 나세요 is a genuine wish of good fortune to someone opening a business.

examples.translation: No way! You actually got in?
This series is an absolute smash.

origin.etymology: From 大舶, a large ship — a merchant vessel coming in was the traditional image of a fortune arriving. The interjection use is much newer than the noun, and belongs to the last few decades.

definitions.text: Whoa; what the — the sound of being briefly stunned. Slightly more negative than 대박, and used for the unwelcome as readily as the impressive.

examples.translation: Oh no — I've left my wallet behind.
Whoa — seriously?
examples.context: The three words are so often chained together that the sequence functions as one reaction.

origin.etymology: An onomatopoeia for a sharp intake of breath, written down and spread through early-2000s online chat and text messaging. It moved from typing into speech, not the other way round.

definitions.text: The best; top. As a suffix it names the champion of a category: 얼짱 (best face), 몸짱 (best body).
Standalone, 짱이야 means 'that's brilliant'. Now reads as slightly older slang — a word that dates the speaker to the 1990s or 2000s.
definitions.note: Still perfectly understood, but a Korean teenager is likelier to say 대박 or 개좋아.

examples.translation: My mum's the best — absolute legend.
He was the best-looking guy in our school.

origin.etymology: Generally traced to 장 (長), 'chief, head', reinforced with a tensed initial consonant — a common Korean way of adding emphasis, as in 쫌 for 좀.

definitions.text: Genuinely entertaining — of a film, a night out, a class. 꿀 ('honey') is a productive intensifier: 꿀팁 is a great tip, 꿀알바 a cushy job.

examples.translation: That film last night was brilliant.
This class is actually fun, so I don't nod off.

origin.etymology: 꿀 ('honey') plus 잼, a clipping of 재미 ('fun'). Built by the abbreviation habit that dominates Korean youth slang.

definitions.text: No fun at all; a dud. Of a film, a joke that died, or a person with no comic timing.
노잼 시기 is a recognised state: a stretch of weeks when nothing amuses you.

examples.translation: That film is a complete waste of time.
I think I'm in one of those phases where nothing's funny.

origin.etymology: English 'no' plus 잼, from 재미 ('fun') — a hybrid of the kind Korean slang builds constantly. The middle grade, 핵노잼 ('nuclear-level unfunny'), is stronger still.

definitions.text: You can do it; keep going. Shouted before an exam, a match, a shift or a difficult conversation. Encouragement, never an instruction to fight.
definitions.note: 화이팅 and 파이팅 are the same word; the second is the spelling the National Institute of Korean Language prefers, the first is what most people write.

examples.translation: Good luck in the exam — you've got this!
Here's to getting through today.
examples.context: A routine message-closer among colleagues, roughly 'chin up, we've got this'.

origin.etymology: From English 'fighting', borrowed through mid-century sport. Japanese ファイト is the same borrowing narrowed the same way, and the two spread in parallel.

definitions.text: Older brother — said by a woman. Extended to any older male she is close to: a friend, a boyfriend, a senior at university.
A man uses 형 (hyeong) for the same relationship, and 누나 (nuna) for an older woman; a woman uses 언니 (eonni).
definitions.note: Strictly gendered by the speaker, not by the person addressed. A man calling another man 오빠 is making a joke.

definitions.text: In fandom it extends to male idols the speaker has never met, which is where the word entered English.

examples.text: 오빠, 이것 좀 들어줄 수 있어?
examples.translation: Could you carry this for me?
examples.context: Said to an older brother, an older male friend or a boyfriend — the word covers all three.

examples.translation: My older brother is doing his military service.

origin.etymology: Korean uses kinship terms as everyday address far more than European languages do, and choosing one is unavoidable: there is no neutral 'you' that works between people of different ages. Learning the four-term grid is a practical necessity, not a cultural nicety.

definitions.text: Older sister — said by a woman, and by extension to any older woman she is friendly with.
Also used to female staff in shops, restaurants and markets regardless of actual age, as a friendly way of getting attention.

examples.translation: Excuse me — do you have this in another size?
examples.context: To a shop assistant. 저기요 is the neutral alternative if you are unsure.

examples.translation: My older sister is a seriously good cook.

definitions.text: Someone senior to you in an institution — school, university, company — by year of entry rather than age. Its pair is 후배 (hubae), the junior.
The relationship carries real obligations: the senior is expected to buy meals and give advice, the junior to be deferential and available.
definitions.note: Entry year, not age, decides it. A 40-year-old who joined last year is junior to a 25-year-old who joined the year before.

examples.translation: One of the older students bought me dinner.
Ask someone senior at work.

definitions.text: A middle-aged woman. Neutral in the third person; said to someone's face it can sting, because it declares her no longer young.
definitions.note: 아주머니 is the polite form and is the safe choice when addressing a stranger. Getting this wrong is a common and memorable error.

definitions.text: Also a cultural type — permed hair, visor, floral trousers, formidable in a queue — affectionately parodied and genuinely admired in roughly equal measure.

examples.translation: Excuse me, could we have some water?
examples.context: The polite form, which is what you should use in a restaurant.

examples.translation: Nobody is tougher than the women who run the market stalls.

definitions.text: A middle-aged man, and the usual way to address a taxi driver or a delivery man. Says plainly that the speaker considers him past youth.
definitions.note: Men in their thirties dislike it intensely. Younger speakers often hedge with 삼촌 ('uncle') to avoid the sting.

examples.translation: Could you pull over here, please?
examples.context: To a taxi driver — entirely standard.

examples.translation: I'm not middle-aged yet, thanks.

definitions.text: The ability to read a room and judge what people actually want without being told. Having it is a compliment; 눈치가 없다, lacking it, is a real criticism.
눈치를 보다 — 'to watch for nunchi' — is to keep an anxious eye on someone's mood before acting, which is as often a burden as a skill.

examples.translation: He genuinely cannot read a room.

examples.text: 상사 눈치 보느라 퇴근을 못 해.
examples.translation: I can't leave the office because I'm watching for my boss's mood.

origin.etymology: Widely described as untranslatable, which overstates it — Japanese 空気を読む is close, and English 'reading the room' is closer than usually admitted. What is distinctive is how explicitly Koreans discuss it as a skill you can have more or less of.

definitions.text: The attachment that builds up between people, or to a place, simply through time spent together — not affection chosen but affection accumulated.
정이 들다 is for it to develop; 정 떨어지다, for it to break, is what happens when someone does something that makes you unable to feel it any more.
definitions.note: It explains behaviour foreigners find puzzling: the shopkeeper adding a free item, the colleague who will not let you pay. That is 정 being demonstrated.

examples.translation: I've grown really attached to this neighbourhood.
After he said that, whatever I felt for him was gone.

origin.etymology: From Sino-Korean 情, 'feeling'. Korean commentary treats it as a defining national emotion; the word itself is ordinary and its use is entirely everyday.

definitions.text: An older person who lectures juniors about how things were done in their day and expects deference for their age alone.
Age is not strictly required: 젊은 꼰대, the 'young kkondae', is a recognised figure — someone two years senior behaving exactly the same way.

examples.translation: Our department head is such a dinosaur.
I really don't want to turn into one of those people.

origin.etymology: Schoolboy slang for a teacher or a father from the 1960s, revived around 2015 as a general term in the public argument about workplace hierarchy. One derivation traces it to French comte via Japanese; it is unverified and probably folk etymology.

definitions.text: Abuse of a position of power over someone dependent on you: a client humiliating a supplier, an executive berating cabin crew, a landlord leaning on a tenant.
A term of public accusation rather than private grumbling. Korean news reports use it directly, and several corporate scandals have been named with it.

examples.translation: That is straightforwardly an abuse of position.
They put out an apology over the bullying allegations.

origin.etymology: 갑 and 을 are the labels for the first and second parties in a Korean contract — Party A and Party B. 갑 came to mean the side with the power, and the suffix -질 (denoting a demeaning activity) does the rest. The word is a piece of legal boilerplate turned into an indictment.

definitions.text: Someone born wealthy, whose start in life was bought for them. Part of a full ranking — 금 (gold), 은 (silver), 동 (bronze), 흙 (dirt) — that Koreans use half-jokingly and half-seriously about their own prospects.

examples.translation: He was born into money, so he's got nothing to worry about.

examples.text: 수저 계급론이 괜히 나온 게 아니야.
examples.translation: There's a reason people talk about the spoon classes.

origin.etymology: A reworking of the English 'born with a silver spoon', which Korean expanded into a graded hierarchy after the 2015 debates about inherited inequality. The English idiom describes one condition; the Korean version describes a class system.

definitions.text: Someone born with nothing to fall back on — the bottom of the spoon hierarchy, and very often a self-description.

examples.translation: I had no safety net, so I started out doing part-time work.
They say effort alone no longer gets you anywhere if you started from nothing.

definitions.text: South Korea seen as a place of hopeless competition: brutal work culture, unaffordable housing, exams that decide a life at eighteen. Bitter rather than playful.
definitions.note: Peaked in the mid-2010s and is now used more retrospectively, but everyone under fifty recognises it instantly.

examples.translation: This is exactly why people call this place hell.
Getting out of the country was the dream.

origin.etymology: English 'hell' plus 조선, the dynasty that ruled Korea until 1910 — the joke being that a rigid, hereditary society never actually ended. Coined online around 2015 and picked up immediately by the national press.

definitions.text: Being paid in experience: the internship, the fashion placement or the studio job that offers exposure and enthusiasm in place of wages.

examples.translation: That company is notorious for paying in exposure.
Unpaid 'passion' work is illegal now.

origin.etymology: 열정 ('passion') plus English 'pay'. Coined around 2014 in a public argument about unpaid internships in fashion and the arts, and now used in labour-law reporting.

definitions.text: A part-time job, and the person doing it. 알바생 is the worker, 알바비 the wage, 꿀알바 a cushy one.

examples.translation: I'm working part-time at a café.
When does the part-time pay come in?

origin.etymology: Clipped from 아르바이트, taken from German Arbeit through Japanese アルバイト during the colonial period. One of many German words that reached Korean by that route rather than directly.

definitions.text: Someone out of work and not currently studying — typically a graduate between things. Usually self-applied and lightly rueful rather than insulting.
definitions.note: 백조 ('white swan') is the jokey female version, a pun on 백수 with the same first syllable.

examples.translation: I've been out of work for six months since graduating.
I'm unemployed, so time is the one thing I have.

origin.etymology: From 白手, 'empty-handed' — hands with nothing in them. The image is of having no work rather than of not doing manual labour.

definitions.text: Fried chicken and beer, taken as a single item. A national institution: eaten in parks, outside convenience stores, at football, and delivered anywhere including the riverbank.

examples.translation: Fried chicken and beer tonight?
Nothing beats chicken and beer by the river.

origin.etymology: 치킨 plus 맥주 ('beer'), first syllables only. Its global spread owes a great deal to the 2014 drama 별에서 온 그대, whose heroine's fondness for it started a chicken boom across Asia.

definitions.text: Soju dropped into beer — Korea's boilermaker. Mixed at the table, often theatrically, and drunk in one.
At a company dinner these arrive by the round, and declining is easier than it used to be but still takes a moment of nerve.

examples.translation: I'll mix you a soju-beer.
The ratio is what makes or breaks it.

origin.etymology: 소주 plus 맥주, first syllables again. The verb used with it is 말다, the same verb as for stirring rice into soup.

definitions.text: The second venue of a night out, moved to as a group: barbecue first, then a bar, then very often karaoke for 삼차.
The numbering is used seriously. Announcing 저는 이차까지만 ('I'll stay through the second round') is the accepted way to set a limit in advance.

examples.translation: Where are we going for round two?
I'll stay for the second round and then head off.

definitions.text: Eating or drinking to clear a hangover. 해장국 is the soup made for it, and 해장술 is the hair-of-the-dog version, which Koreans discuss with more enthusiasm than doctors would like.

examples.translation: Let's go get soup and sort this hangover out.
Bean sprout soup is the best hangover cure there is.

origin.etymology: From 解酲, 'to undo drunkenness'. That a language has a dedicated verb for the morning-after meal, and a whole restaurant category serving it around the clock, says something about the drinking culture it belongs to.

definitions.text: Someone who can drink enormous amounts — a fish, in the English idiom, though Korean scales it up to a whale.

examples.translation: He drinks like a fish.
Drinking with him always ruins the next day.

definitions.text: Eating a meal alone. Once faintly shameful in a culture built on shared dishes, now ordinary — restaurants advertise single-seat counters for it.

examples.translation: I ate lunch by myself today.
There are far more restaurants that are comfortable to eat alone in now.

origin.etymology: 혼자 ('alone') plus 밥 ('rice, meal'). Part of a whole family — 혼술, 혼영, 혼행 — that appeared in the mid-2010s along with the rise of single-person households.

definitions.text: Drinking alone, by choice and usually at home — a beer with a film rather than a problem.
Genuinely new as an acceptable activity. Korean drinking has historically been collective, down to the rule that you do not pour your own glass.
definitions.note: That rule still holds in company: you fill others' glasses and let someone fill yours.

examples.translation: I'm going to have a quiet drink at home tonight.
Drinking alone isn't so bad, actually.

definitions.text: A broadcast of someone eating a very large meal while talking to the audience. Korean in origin and now a global streaming genre under its Korean name.

examples.translation: Watching eating shows before bed just makes me hungry.
That YouTuber made their name doing eating broadcasts.

origin.etymology: 먹는 ('eating') plus 방송 ('broadcast'). It began on the Korean streaming platform AfreecaTV around 2010, and is often linked to the rise of single-person households — company for a solitary meal.

definitions.text: A restaurant worth travelling for. Not fine dining — a 맛집 is more often a two-table place with one dish and a queue.

examples.translation: Tell me somewhere good to eat round here.
We drove an hour to get to a place worth eating at.

definitions.text: Unbelievably tasty. Very common among young people, and technically obscene — 존 is a clipping of a crude word.
definitions.note: Most speakers no longer feel the origin, but it is not something to say to a client or an older relative. The initials JMT are the polite dodge.

examples.translation: The tteokbokki here is unreal.
This combination is elite, agreed?

origin.etymology: From 존나, an intensifier derived from a vulgar term for male anatomy, plus 맛 ('taste'). The same 존 appears in 존예 ('stunning') and 개 serves the same intensifying function more mildly.

definitions.text: The stage before a relationship: more than friends, nothing declared. 썸 타다 is to be in it, and 썸남/썸녀 is the person you are in it with.
A named stage rather than a vague one. Korean dating turns on a declaration — 사귀자, 'let's go out' — and 썸 is everything that comes before it.

examples.translation: We're in that not-quite-dating stage.
It never got past the almost-something stage and fizzled out.

origin.etymology: From English 'something' — as in 'there's something going on there' — clipped to one syllable. Popularised by a 2014 song of the same name.

definitions.text: Playing hard to get, in both directions: replying late, showing interest and then withdrawing it, keeping the other person guessing.

examples.translation: Stop playing games and just say it.
I'm exhausted by all the back and forth.

origin.etymology: 밀고 당기기, 'pushing and pulling', compressed to two syllables — the standard Korean abbreviation pattern applied to a whole phrase.

definitions.text: Keeping several interested people on the hook at once — enough attention to hold them, never enough to commit. A clear accusation, not a neutral description.

examples.translation: He's stringing people along — don't fall for it.
I think I was being kept on the back burner.

origin.etymology: The metaphor is fully worked out: the fish are the admirers, the pond is the messaging app, and the manager feeds them just enough to keep them swimming.

definitions.text: The lurch your heart gives at something adorable or unexpectedly attractive — a puppy, a smile, a line in a drama.

examples.translation: That scene properly got me.
Saw a photo of the dog and my heart went.

origin.etymology: 심장 ('heart') plus 쿵, the onomatopoeia for a heavy thud. Korean builds a great deal of vocabulary from sound words, and 쿵 is the same thump used for a door slamming.

definitions.text: Performed cuteness: a softened voice, a slight pout, a wheedling tone used to charm someone into agreeing with you.
A skill people are asked to demonstrate on demand — 애교 해봐 is a standard request on Korean variety shows and, less comfortably, at company dinners.
definitions.note: Not confined to women, though the expectation falls on them much harder.

examples.translation: Go on, do the cute thing.
I have absolutely no charm-offensive in me.

definitions.text: A warm, decent-looking man — the kind who makes a room feel easier rather than the spectacular kind. 훈녀 is the female equivalent.
Explicitly not about perfect features: the compliment is about the impression he leaves.

examples.translation: The new teacher is lovely-looking in that warm way.
I'd take approachable over handsome any day.

origin.etymology: 훈훈하다, 'warming, heartening' — the word used for a gently heated room — plus 남, 'man'. The metaphor is temperature, not looks.

definitions.text: Someone exceptionally good-looking — literally the best face in a given group. 몸짱 is the same for physique.
definitions.note: Early-2000s vintage and now faintly dated; it evokes the era of internet photo rankings it came from.

examples.translation: Apparently she was known as the best-looking girl in school.
I've joined a gym to get in shape.

origin.etymology: 얼굴 ('face') plus 짱 ('best'). It spread through early-2000s photo-ranking sites, several of which launched careers — a few of Korea's best-known actors were 얼짱 first.

definitions.text: An insider: the person who knows everyone, is at every gathering and is never short of plans.
인싸템 is an item everyone has, 인싸력 is the capacity for it — the root is productive.

examples.translation: She knows absolutely everyone.
Apparently this is the thing everyone's got right now.

origin.etymology: English 'insider', Koreanised and clipped to two syllables. Coined around 2018 alongside its opposite 아싸.

definitions.text: An outsider: not in the group, eating alone, not on the messaging thread. Usually self-applied, and worn with a certain defiance.
definitions.note: Not to be confused with the identical-sounding 아싸! meaning 'yes!' — an unrelated cheer, distinguished only by context and delivery.

examples.translation: I was a total loner at university.
Being on the outside has its comforts.

origin.etymology: English 'outsider', clipped the same way as 인싸 and coined as its deliberate counterpart.

definitions.text: The moment a room goes cold — a joke that lands wrong, a subject nobody wanted raised, and the silence that follows.

examples.translation: The second he said it, the whole room went quiet.
Don't kill the mood.

origin.etymology: 갑자기 분위기 싸해짐 — 'the atmosphere suddenly turned cold' — reduced to one syllable per word. A clear demonstration of how far Korean abbreviation will compress a sentence.

definitions.text: Going to pieces — the blank, reeling state after bad news, a disastrous exam or a file lost an hour before a deadline. Everyday and usually not clinical.

examples.translation: I bombed the exam and I'm in bits.
The file vanished and I completely lost it.

origin.etymology: English 'mental' plus 붕괴 ('collapse'). The related 멘탈 갑 is its opposite — someone unshakeable.

definitions.text: To be seriously wound up. Much stronger than 짜증나 — closer to 'livid' — and coarse enough to be out of place at work or with anyone older.
definitions.note: Fine among friends, genuinely inappropriate in front of a senior colleague or a parent.

examples.translation: I'm so furious I can't even speak.
Hearing that makes my blood boil.

origin.etymology: From 빡, a sound word for a sharp crack or blow, with the sense of something snapping inside the head.

definitions.text: That's irritating; this is getting on my nerves. The everyday word for low-grade annoyance, and extremely common.

examples.translation: Oh, this is doing my head in.
Rain. Brilliant.

definitions.text: Utterly revolting; can't stand it. Strong language, mostly written, and applied to food, behaviour and — in online arguments — to people.
definitions.note: Aimed at a person it is genuinely hostile, and 혐오 is the word Korean uses for hate speech.

examples.translation: That scene was absolutely stomach-turning.
Mint chocolate: vile.
examples.context: A long-running and entirely unserious internet argument in Korea.

origin.etymology: 극도로 혐오스럽다 ('extremely repugnant') cut to its first syllables, following the standard abbreviation pattern.

definitions.text: Hopeless; beyond fixing. Of a situation with no way out, or a person who will not be reasoned with.

examples.translation: There is genuinely no way out of this.
He's a lost cause.
examples.context: 답이 없다 is the unabbreviated form, and is what you would say out loud.

origin.etymology: English 'no' plus 답 ('answer'), on the model of 노잼. The image is of an exam question with no correct option.

definitions.text: A moment of clean, fizzing satisfaction: the character who finally says the thing, the complaint that gets answered properly, the villain who gets what is coming.
사이다 발언 is a remark that cuts straight through a situation everyone else was tiptoeing around.

examples.translation: That scene was so satisfying.
I applauded — someone finally said it.

origin.etymology: The drink, understood as the thing that clears a blocked chest. It exists entirely as the opposite of 고구마, and the pair is one of the neatest metaphors in Korean slang.

definitions.text: Something maddeningly stuck: a plot where nobody says what they obviously should, a colleague who will not come to the point, a process that goes nowhere.

examples.translation: This drama is unbearably frustrating.
It's like swallowing a hundred dry sweet potatoes.

origin.etymology: A dry sweet potato eaten without a drink sticks in the throat — the physical sensation of the thing that will not go down. 사이다 is what you reach for to clear it, which is exactly why it is the opposite term.

definitions.text: Laughter in text — the Korean 'haha'. The number of characters scales with the laugh, from a polite single ㅋ to a screen of them.
ㅎㅎ is the softer, warmer version, closer to a smile than a laugh, and is the safer choice when messaging someone senior.
definitions.note: A bare ㅋ on its own can read as curt or sarcastic. Two or three are the neutral default.

examples.translation: That's actually hilarious 😂
Sure, understood 🙂
examples.context: ㅎㅎ softens a work message without making it unprofessional.

origin.etymology: ㅋ is a bare Hangul consonant, the sound k, standing in for the sound of laughing. Writing consonants alone this way is a whole layer of Korean texting: ㅇㅇ for yes, ㄴㄴ for no, ㅊㅊ for congratulations.

definitions.text: Crying — the Hangul vowel ㅠ read as a pictogram of a face with tears running down. Used for real disappointment and for very small ones alike.

examples.translation: Working late again 😭
Tickets are all gone 😢

origin.etymology: Purely visual, like Japanese 草: the two descending strokes of ㅠ look like tears. ㅜ is the same idea with a single stream.

definitions.text: Oh dear; goodness me; oof. Covers physical effort, mild dismay, sympathy and exasperation, and is most associated with older speakers.
Also the traditional cry of mourning, which is why it can carry real weight in the right setting.

examples.translation: Oof — my back.
Oh no — what on earth has happened here?

definitions.text: What do I do?; oh no. A cry of helplessness, said aloud to nobody in particular as often as to a listener.
Frequently misspelled 어떻해 even by native speakers. The correct form contracts 어떻게 해.
definitions.note: 어떻게 (how) and 어떡해 (what do I do) are pronounced almost identically and mixing them up is Korea's most-discussed spelling error.

examples.translation: Oh no — I've cracked my screen.
What am I going to do?

definitions.text: Really; genuinely. The commonest intensifier in spoken Korean, dropped in front of almost anything.
On its own, with rising intonation, 'seriously?'. Flat and drawn out, it is an expression of exasperation: 진짜… means 'I don't believe this'.

examples.translation: This is really good.
Seriously? When did that happen?

origin.etymology: From 眞, 'true', plus a native suffix. Its more formal counterpart 정말 means the same thing and sounds noticeably more careful.

definitions.text: Totally; completely. Grammatically a noun meaning 'completeness', used adverbially in casual speech in a way prescriptivists object to and everyone under forty does anyway.
definitions.note: 완전히 is the textbook adverb. Bare 완전 marks the speech as informal and young.

examples.translation: That is absolutely incredible.
Totally my sort of thing.

definitions.text: Just; no particular reason. Declines to explain, politely: asked why you did something, 그냥 is a complete and accepted answer.
Also 'as is, without doing anything about it' — 그냥 둬, 'leave it'.

examples.translation: 'Why did you call?' 'No reason.'
I'd rather just stay in.

definitions.text: Roughly; approximately; good enough. Of an estimate, and of work done to the minimum standard that will pass.
Whether it is a criticism depends entirely on who is describing whose work.

examples.text: 대충 이 정도면 될 것 같아.
examples.translation: This much should do it, roughly.
Don't just knock it out — do it properly.

definitions.text: Respect other people's taste. Said to someone sneering at what you like — the Korean equivalent of 'let people enjoy things'.

examples.translation: Could you just let people like what they like?
Liking mint choc chip is a valid taste, thanks.

origin.etymology: 취향 존중, 'respect for taste', abbreviated to one syllable each. 안물안궁 — 'didn't ask, not curious' — is the adjacent put-down built the same way.

definitions.text: KakaoTalk, and by extension any message sent on it — which in Korea means essentially all messages. 카톡해 is 'message me'.
The notification sound is itself a cultural fixture, and 카톡왔숑 is onomatopoeia for it.

examples.translation: I'll message you later.
I've posted the announcement in the group chat.
examples.context: 단톡방, from 단체 카톡방, is a group chat — and the source of a particular kind of workplace dread.

origin.etymology: 카카오톡 clipped to two syllables. KakaoTalk's dominance in Korea is close to total, which is why the brand name became the generic verb.

definitions.text: A selfie. Korean coined its own word years before English settled on one, and kept it.
셀카봉 is a selfie stick; 셀기꾼 — 셀카 plus 사기꾼 ('fraudster') — is someone whose selfies look nothing like them.

examples.translation: Let's just get one selfie.
With selfies, the angle is everything.

origin.etymology: 셀프 카메라, 'self camera' — an English-shaped compound built in Korean that no English speaker says. Korea's early camera phones meant the word was in wide use by the mid-2000s.

definitions.text: Lurking: reading a forum or a group chat regularly without ever posting.

examples.translation: I only lurk on that forum.
I'm just reading the group chat, not joining in.

origin.etymology: 눈 ('eye') plus the English -ing ending, borrowed as a productive Korean suffix. 채팅 and 미팅 came the same way.

definitions.text: Studying flat out. Said of exam season, and used as an encouragement — 열공해 is 'work hard'.

Korea's exam culture gives this word more weight than an English translation suggests: the 수능 university entrance test is a single day the whole country arranges itself around, down to delaying flights during the listening section.

examples.translation: I'm buried in studying at the moment.
Exams are close — get your head down.

origin.etymology: 열심히 공부하다, 'study hard', cut to its first syllables.

definitions.text: Restorative rest: a quiet café, a walk, a slow television programme. The English word borrowed and narrowed to mean recovering from ordinary exhaustion rather than from illness.
definitions.note: 힐링 영화 and 힐링 예능 are recognised genres — media made specifically to be undemanding.

examples.translation: Looking at the sea is restoring me.
I need the weekend to recover.

origin.etymology: From English 'healing', which took off as a buzzword around 2012 in reaction to the exhaustion 헬조선 names. The two words belong to the same conversation from opposite ends.
